strengths: Systematic and well-motivated analysis: Clear computational cost breakdown and insightful identification of the 'information migration' phenomenon that validates the two-stage design

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 benchmarks (8 image + 4 video), dual model scales (7B/13B), strong empirical results with consistent improvements across all tasks, and thorough ablation studies
Practical and broadly applicable: Training-free, architecture-agnostic approach with no retraining required; plug-and-play compatibility with efficient attention operators
Strong empirical results at extreme compression: Achieves 95.1% performance with 90% token pruning, outperforming second-best by 2.4%, with good cross-model transferability
Valuable insights: Identifies and articulates specific limitations of prior attention-based methods (positional bias) and proposes well-motivated alternative based on token diversity
weaknesses: Unvalidated theoretical foundation: The orthogonality proof (Appendix B) critically assumes visual and text embeddings occupy orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), but this assumption is never empirically verified on actual LVLMs, undermining the theoretical justification

Incomplete overhead analysis: Stage 1 requires O(n²) pairwise similarity computation and Stage 2 requires attention computation at multiple layers; computational overhead is acknowledged but not quantified, leaving unclear whether reported speedups fully account for this cost

Limited algorithmic novelty: Greedy k-center is well-established (1985); cross-modal attention pruning is not new; contribution primarily lies in engineering combination of existing techniques with partially empirical design choices

Unprincipled hyperparameter selection: Key parameters (k=288, layer selection at L/2,5L/8,6L/8,7L/8, threshold τ=0.03) lack principled justification and appear to require task/model-specific tuning, raising questions about generalizability
Limited architectural diversity: All experiments conducted exclusively on LLaVA-NeXT; evaluation on other LVLM architectures (Qwen-VL, DeepSeek-VL2) would strengthen generalization claims
Stage 2 provides marginal gains: Table 4 shows Stage 2 alone yields only 6.5% speedup; the 2.6× speedup is dominated by Stage 1, somewhat misrepresenting the two-stage contribution balance

Concurrent related work underexplored: DivPrune (Ref. [2]) uses similar diversity-based selection; relationship and distinctions are not discussed, making novelty assessment relative to concurrent work difficult

Unexplained anomalies in results: Video benchmarks show performance exceeding baseline (105.0% vs. 100%), attributed vaguely to 'reduced interference'; requires deeper analysis to validate whether this represents genuine performance gain
Missing sensitivity analyses: No exploration of alternative diversity metrics, attention-based Stage 1 variants, or pivot selection strategy sensitivity; these would strengthen robustness claims
Reproducibility limitations: No code availability mentioned; computational overhead implementation details unclear; full reproducibility without code is challenging

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: identifies concrete limitations of attention-based pruning (positional bias) and discovers the 'information migration' phenomenon with strong empirical evidence (Figures 1-2)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 12 benchmarks and multiple model sizes (7B, 13B) with strong results (95.1% performance at 10% retention), outperforming baselines by 2.4-2.9%
Principled two-stage design with theoretical grounding: orthogonal decomposition of intra-modal and cross-modal redundancy justified in Appendix B with covariance proof
Training-free, plug-and-play approach with good generalization: better transfer to 13B models than competitors (FastV, SparseVLM) without retraining
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-6, Appendix C) quantifying individual contributions and careful analysis of design choices (threshold τ, layer selection)
Well-presented with clear examples comparing diversity-based vs attention-based retention; good visualizations of token distributions (Figure 7) and qualitative comparisons (Figure 6)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: greedy k-center is standard (Gonzalez 1985), layer selection via attention ratios is straightforward, with primary contribution being the combination of existing techniques with domain insights; concurrent work (DivPrune) proposes similar ideas

Significant unquantified computational overhead in Stage 1: k-center requires iterative pairwise similarity computations acknowledged as limitation but not quantified; actual speedup (1.9×) vs claimed FLOPs reduction (80.9%) suggests ~43% efficiency loss to overhead

Strong theoretical assumptions with limited empirical validation: orthogonality assumption (W_V^T W_T = 0) is strong and may not hold in learned embeddings; no verification that LLaVA-NeXT satisfies this assumption

Stage 2 provides limited practical impact: contributes only 6.5% speedup alone (Table 4); acknowledged that benefits limited to short outputs in current benchmarks; limited evaluation on longer-form generation tasks despite this being the claimed use case

Hyperparameter tuning required with limited generalization guidance: threshold τ = 0.03 and layer indices (L/2, 5L/8, 6L/8, 7L/8) appear heuristic; no systematic approach for selecting these for new models without expensive ablation studies

Pivot token selection contradicts stated motivation: Stage 1 criticizes attention-based methods for positional bias, yet uses [CLS] attention for pivot selection; justification for why [CLS] is reliable here while other attention patterns are not is unclear

Incomplete baseline comparisons: FastV and SparseVLM excluded from 13B experiments due to 'transferability issues' preventing fair comparison; limited analysis of why ToDRE generalizes better than these methods

Limited failure mode analysis and scope: single successful example (Figure 1) without discussing when attention-based pruning might be preferable; evaluated only on LLaVA-NeXT variants, not other major LVLMs (Qwen-VL, DeepSeek-VL); no adversarial robustness analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem analysis: Clear identification of limitations in attention-based and similarity-based pruning, with compelling empirical evidence for information migration phenomenon
Strong and consistent empirical results: Outperforms or matches competing methods across 4 models and 12 benchmarks; achieves 2.6× speedup while maintaining 95% performance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough ablation studies, cross-model evaluation, clear Stage 1 vs Stage 2 breakdown, extensive supplementary material with theoretical analysis
Practical and deployable: Training-free, architecture-agnostic framework compatible with efficient attention operators; easy integration into existing systems
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with informative visualizations and detailed supplementary material
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Uses existing greedy max-sum diversification algorithm; two-stage design decomposes into straightforward techniques (diversity selection + layer pruning); theoretical analysis assumes orthogonal embedding spaces that may not hold for end-to-end trained LVLMs

Stage 2 contribution is marginal: Only 0.1-0.2% performance improvement and 8-9% additional speedup from Stage 2; Stage 1 alone achieves most efficiency gains, somewhat contradicting emphasis on two-stage design

Minimal improvement over concurrent work (DivPrune): Achieves only 1-2% gains over DivPrune on many benchmarks; at 10% retention on videos, essentially identical performance (100.7% vs 100.9%); distinction from DivPrune unclear

Ad-hoc hyperparameter selection: Layer selection at 7L/8 and threshold τ=0.10 appear task/model-specific with no principled approach for new models; random pivot selection performs comparably to [CLS]-based selection, suggesting limited importance

Limited analysis of method applicability: No discussion of failure cases; paper acknowledges most benchmarks require short answers limiting observed decoding stage gains; claimed benefits for longer generation are not empirically validated

Incomplete information migration analysis: Information migration observed after Stage 1 pruning has already removed most tokens; no verification that phenomenon holds across all tested models; insufficient analysis of whether removing all visual tokens at one layer prevents earlier use when needed

Experimental scope limitations: All experiments on single GPU (RTX 3090); excluded comparisons justify exclusions but limit fairness assessment; no empirical validation of theoretical orthogonal subspace assumption
